phlegmatic

/fleg-MAT-ik/ - the stress falls on MAT · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Phlegmatic means calm and unemotional; not easily excited or upset.

Marta, the building's phlegmatic superintendent, greeted the burst pipe on the fourth floor the way she greeted everything — 'Right,' she said, and went for the wrench.

Worked Example

Referee Odum stayed phlegmatic through the cup final's worst brawl: he separated the captains, booked three players in his tidy handwriting, and restarted the match ninety seconds later, pulse apparently untouched.

Phlegmatic is more precise than 'calm' because calm can describe anyone's good afternoon; phlegmatic names a temperament — a person built so level that emergencies, insults, and jackpots all arrive to the same mild nod. It often carries a hint of coolness: the phlegmatic don't celebrate much either.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

unflappable: Unflappable means impossible to rattle, whatever arrives — it reports the result. Phlegmatic names the temperament underneath: a person built so level that the surge never comes in the first place. Someone can train themselves unflappable for a job; the phlegmatic were simply issued that way.

composed: Composed means your feelings are held in check right now — control that takes effort, the slow breath before the speech. Phlegmatic is composed as a permanent setting, no breath needed, because nothing is surging underneath. Anyone can be composed for an hour; the phlegmatic are level for life.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

excitable: sparks at the smallest provocation

panicky: tips into alarm the moment plans wobble

Where it sits · how built-in the composure is — calm → phlegmatic → stony

calm vs. phlegmatic: Calm can describe anyone's quiet hour — milder than phlegmatic, which is calm installed at the factory, running in every weather.

stony vs. phlegmatic: Stony goes further than phlegmatic: past unexcitable into unreadable, with even the warmth switched off.

Build the Word

The pieces

Root — phlegm

Root — phlegm: the cold, moist bodily humor of old medicine

Suffix — -atic

Suffix — -atic: characteristic of (a form of -ic)

Put it together

Put it together: Phlegm (the cold, slow humor of medieval medicine) + -atic (characteristic of) = having phlegm's character. Doctors once sorted temperaments by which of four bodily fluids ruled you, and too much phlegm was said to make you cool, slow to stir, hard to alarm. The chemistry was nonsense, but the portrait survived: the phlegmatic type answers a fire alarm the way others answer a doorbell.

Word Choice

clinical / character-sketch

Phlegmatic is a temperament word for character sketches — pilots, nurses, goalkeepers who cannot be hurried into feeling. Plain 'calm' covers a moment; phlegmatic claims the whole personality. Beside its unit-mate fatalistic, note the difference in engine: the phlegmatic person stays level and keeps working, while the fatalistic one may be excitable enough — they've just decided the outcome is out of everyone's hands.
